questions.question: Andrija Mohorovičić gathered the seismograph records of an earthquake that shook the Kupa Valley, in Croatia, on 8 October 1909, from 41 stations. Out to about 240 kilometres from the quake, each station recorded a single P-wave, the fastest kind of earthquake wave. Farther out, many stations recorded two P-waves, and the first to arrive was one that no nearer station had picked up. What did Mohorovičić conclude?
questions.answer: Below a certain depth, rock carries the waves faster
choices: Below a certain depth, rock carries the waves faster
The quake broke twice, at two depths, moments apart
Below a certain depth, the rock is melted, like magma
Strong waves outrun weak ones over long distances
questions.context: Waves that dipped into the faster rock below ran along it and climbed back up, and beyond about 240 kilometres they overtook the waves that stayed in the shallower rock, though their route was longer; Mohorovičić showed that the two were one kind of wave arriving by different paths. Two shocks would have sent two waves to the nearer stations too. He put the boundary about 54 kilometres down, and it is now called the Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho: the base of the crust.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science teaches that seismic waves change speed and bend at boundaries inside Earth, and the Moho is the first boundary they revealed.

questions.question: A great earthquake sends two main kinds of wave through Earth. P-waves squeeze and stretch the rock along their path, while S-waves shake it from side to side. Seismographs across much of the far side of Earth record P-waves from the quake but no S-waves that have come straight through, and from that shadow seismologists concluded that the outer core is liquid. Why can an S-wave not cross a liquid?
questions.answer: A liquid does not spring back when pushed sideways
choices: A liquid does not spring back when pushed sideways
A liquid's great density smothers any sideways shaking
A liquid's heat breaks up any sideways shaking
A liquid's particles sit too far apart to pass the wave on
questions.context: An S-wave travels only through material that pushes back when it is sheared, as solid rock does; a liquid simply flows aside, so the wave dies out at the core's edge. A liquid does spring back when it is squeezed, which is why P-waves cross the outer core, though they slow down and bend where they enter it. The solid mantle just above the core is hot and dense, yet it carries S-waves.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that S-waves cannot travel through liquid and that their shadow is the evidence for a liquid outer core; the reason a liquid stops them is what makes that evidence work.

questions.question: Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist, studied the records of a strong earthquake in New Zealand in 1929. Earth's core was then thought to be liquid all through. It slows P-waves and bends them away from a wide shadow zone on the far side of the planet, yet two stations in Russia, well inside that zone, had recorded unusually strong P-waves from the quake. What did Lehmann propose in 1936 to explain them?
questions.answer: A smaller core inside the core, where waves travel faster
choices: A smaller core inside the core, where waves travel faster
A smaller core inside the core, where waves travel more slowly
A layer at the bottom of the mantle, where waves travel faster
A layer at the top of the core, where waves travel more slowly
questions.context: P-waves that reach the inner core speed up, and the change of speed at its edge bends some of them out into the shadow zone, where the Russian stations caught them. Beno Gutenberg, Charles Richter and Harold Jeffreys took up Lehmann's idea within a few years. Others argued from 1940 that the inner core is solid iron, and studies of the whole Earth ringing after great earthquakes confirmed by 1971 that it is solid.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science tells Lehmann's inner core as the classic case of a few odd readings overturning a model of Earth's interior; here the waves' change of speed, not the 6th-grade list of layers, decides the answer.

questions.question: Harry Hess's idea of sea-floor spreading, published in 1962, says that new ocean floor forms along the mid-ocean ridges and moves slowly away on either side. The drilling ship Glomar Challenger tested it across the ridge in the South Atlantic in 1968 and 1969, at sites from near its crest to more than 1,600 kilometres away. At each site, scientists dated the fossils in the lowest mud, the layer resting on the sea floor's rock. Which result would have counted most against Hess?
questions.answer: The lowest mud about the same age at every site
choices: The lowest mud about the same age at every site
The lowest mud older at sites farther from the crest
The mud thin near the crest and thicker farther out
The ages climbing at the same pace on both sides
questions.context: The first mud settles on new rock soon after it forms, so if the floor moves out from the crest, the lowest mud must be older the farther out it lies. It was: about 11 million years old at a site some 200 kilometres out and about 76 million at one more than 1,600 kilometres out, the floor moving away at about 2 centimetres a year, in step with the ages read from the sea floor's magnetic stripes. Mud of one age everywhere would have meant a sea floor made all at once.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade earth science (NGSS HS-ESS1-5) has students use the ages of ocean crust to test plate motion, and the drilling cores were the direct test.

questions.question: Zircon crystals take in uranium as they grow but shut lead out, so any lead inside one was made there by the decay of its uranium. Uranium-235 decays into lead-207 with a half-life of about 700 million years. A geologist counts three atoms of lead-207 in a zircon for every atom of uranium-235 still left in it. How old is the crystal?
choices: About 1.4 billion years
About 2.1 billion years
About 2.8 billion years
About 700 million years
questions.context: Three lead atoms for every uranium atom left means a quarter of the uranium remains: half was gone after one half-life and half of the rest after a second, so two half-lives, about 1.4 billion years, have passed. Three lead atoms do not mean three half-lives, which would leave only an eighth, with seven lead atoms for every uranium atom. Because zircon starts with no lead, its clock begins at zero when the crystal forms.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders (NGSS HS-ESS1-6) work out ages from half-lives, and a count of daughter atoms against parent atoms is the form real dating takes.

questions.question: A zircon can lie kilometres underground for billions of years, through great heat and crushing pressure, while the uranium in it decays into lead. Physicists have tested radioactive decay in great heat and under great pressure, and found that its rate hardly changes. Why is a radioactive clock so hard to disturb?
questions.answer: Decay happens in the nucleus, which heat and pressure barely touch
choices: Decay happens in the nucleus, which heat and pressure barely touch
Decay happens in the outer electrons, which the crystal holds firmly in place
Decay is shielded from heat by the crystal packed around each atom
Decay is far too slow a process for heat to hurry it along
questions.context: Heat, pressure and chemistry act on an atom's outer electrons, while the nucleus sits deep inside, buffered by them, so the decay rate stays fixed. Only decay that captures one of the atom's own electrons can shift, and then usually by less than 1 percent, so a clock that has lain in hot rock can still be trusted. The crystal matters for another reason: it keeps uranium and lead from being added or lost.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science contrasts nuclear change with chemical change, and a decay rate that does not change is the assumption every radiometric age rests on.

questions.question: Lord Kelvin worked out Earth's age in 1862 as the time a hot young planet would need to cool to its present state, reckoning back from how fast rock grows warmer with depth. He put it at 20 to 400 million years, and later at only 20 to 40 million. Pierre Curie and Albert Laborde found in 1903 that radium gives off enough heat to melt its own weight of ice in under an hour. Which of Kelvin's assumptions did that discovery undercut?
questions.answer: That Earth makes no new heat of its own inside
choices: That Earth makes no new heat of its own inside
That Earth began as a ball of melted rock
That Earth's heat seeps out only through solid rock
That Earth's rock is alike all the way down
questions.context: Rocks hold radioactive uranium, thorium and potassium, which make about half the heat now flowing out of Earth, so the planet cools far more slowly than Kelvin's sum allowed. His other flaw, pointed out by John Perry in 1895, was the rigid interior: rock deep inside slowly flows, carrying heat upward far faster than still rock can conduct it, and modern assessments count that the larger error. Radioactivity also gave a better clock, and Bertram Boltwood's uranium-lead ages of 1907 ran, once refined, from 410 million to 2.2 billion years.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that a calculation is only as good as its assumptions, and Kelvin's cooling Earth is the famous case undone by a new discovery.

questions.question: Clair Patterson plotted the lead in five meteorites, three stony and two of iron, on a graph of one kind of lead against another. The five lay along one straight line, and its slope gave their age: about 4.55 billion years, he reported in 1956. He also measured the lead in mud from the deep-sea floor, and it fell on the very same line. What did that show?
questions.answer: Earth formed at the same time as the meteorites
choices: Earth formed at the same time as the meteorites
The mud is as old as the meteorites are
Earth's own rocks are as old as the meteorites
Earth and the meteorites hold the same amount of lead
questions.context: Deep-sea mud was taken to stand for the lead of Earth as a whole, and lying on the meteorites' line meant that Earth's lead had been building up from the same start for the same length of time. The line sets one kind of lead against another, not how much lead each sample holds, and it dates none of Earth's rocks: the mud itself is young, and Earth's oldest rocks, remade over the ages by moving plates and weathering, are only about 4 billion years old. Later work has moved Patterson's figure little: Earth's age is now given as 4.54 billion years, give or take 50 million.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders (NGSS HS-ESS1-6) learn that Earth's age comes from meteorites, and the shared lead line is how the meteorites' age was tied to Earth.

questions.question: Lead from the air and dust of his laboratory kept spoiling Clair Patterson's lead measurements until he built a clean room to keep it out. Robert Kehoe, chief medical adviser of the company that made the lead additive for petrol, held that lead in the human body is normal and that low levels do no harm. Patterson came to think that most of the lead in the air, and in people, was not natural at all. Which of his findings counted most against Kehoe?
questions.answer: Recent snow in Greenland held far more lead than ancient snow
choices: Recent snow in Greenland held far more lead than ancient snow
Fresh snow in Greenland held lead that had fallen out of the air
Lead turned up even in the hair growing on his own head
Meteorites and the most ancient rocks held lead of their own
questions.context: Snow piles up in yearly layers, so Greenland's ice keeps a dated record of the lead in the air, and the recent snow held some 200 times as much lead as snow that fell in ancient times. Lead in fresh snow, in hair or in old rocks shows only that lead is there, not when it came, so none of those finds could tell lead that had always been there from lead added since.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks which evidence can tell two explanations apart, and the dated ice layers, a comparison across time, are what Kehoe's claim could not survive.

52abdff309.why: Judge low: the three wrong choices shared one 'too ...' frame and the key alone broke it. Mixed the frames (density smothers, heat breaks up, particles too far apart), key and context unchanged.

ea3867c90d.why: Judge high: the key was decided by the T2 layers fact (a smaller core inside the core). Now two inner-core choices differ only in faster against slower, so the shadow-zone reasoning decides. The stem says the core was then thought liquid all through (F27) and no longer says 'outer core', which hinted at an inner one. Fact-check uncertain: the context no longer says Lehmann held the core solid; others argued solid iron from 1940 and it was confirmed by 1971.

03b05a0831.why: Fact-check uncertain: the sources give different site distances (191 or 221 km, 1,617 or 1,686 km), so the context says 'some 200 kilometres' and 'more than 1,600 kilometres' and 'about 76 million' (F28).

5c954521d4.why: Judge medium: the stem ruled out 'heat and pressure cancel'. Replaced it with the nucleus-against-electrons confusion, parallel to the key; the context already explains it.

09ef5130b7.why: Judge medium: 'the meteorites broke away from Earth' also fitted the shared lead line, and so did 'meteorites had sprinkled their lead over the sea floor' (meteoritic lead in the mud would lie on the line too). Replaced both with choices the evidence rules out: Earth's own rocks as old as the meteorites (F22) and the same amount of lead (the line plots isotope ratios, F29). Context says why each is wrong.

975f753f0c.why: Judge medium (stance and lane): context trimmed to how Patterson knew; the funding, the 1971 panel, the 1996 ban and the blood-lead fall are gone. Judge low: 'most of that lead' now 'most of the lead in the air, and in people' (F30). Fact-check soft spot: the rise is given as some 200 times since ancient times, with no timing claim (F31).
